newsitem.title: USA: Conrail stockholders reject CSX merger plan.
newsitem.headline: Conrail stockholders reject CSX merger plan.

text.p: Conrail shareholders derailed the railroad's planned $9.3 billion merger with CSX Corp., rejecting a key provision that would have enabled the deal to proceed, handing a victory to rival bidder Norfolk Southern Corp.
The defeat in a vote at a special shareholders meeting here could create a stalemate between Conrail-CSX and Norfolk Southern, which is pursuing a hostile $10.3 billion bid for Conrail.
Conrail Chairman David LeVan said Conrail would schedule a new shareholder vote. He did not specify a date.
"We will reschedule the meeting. We will move on. We have to get out and sell the value of this transaction," he said.

Norfolk Southern Chief Executive Officer David Goode said at least 53 percent of Conrail's outstanding shares were voted against the measure to exempt Conrail from a Pennsylvania law that would require CSX to pay all cash for Conrail.

The waiver would have let CSX complete its $110-a-share cash tender offer to raise its Conrail stake to 40 percent from the current 19.9 percent and give it effective control of Conrail. CSX planned to offer stock for the rest of Conrail, bringing the deal's total value to about $104 a share, based on Thursday's stock prices.
Norfolk, Va.-based Norfolk Southern has bid $115 a share in cash for all Conrail shares.
Speaking at a news conference after the Conrail shareholders meeting, Goode said the vote indicated shareholders "overwhelmingly" defeated the measure.
Norfolk Southern's Goode said any future talks with Philadelphia-based Conrail and Richmond, Va.-based CSX would have to be based on his company's offer of $115 per share.
CSX said it was confident it would prevail in its planned merger with Conrail.

"We have no intention of amending or altering our merger agreement in any way in light of this apparent vote," CSX Chairman John Snow said. He said the managements of CSX and Conrail were preparing to present the merger to the federal Surface Transportation Board in March.
Conrail's LeVan had insisted before the vote that the railroad was committed to its proposed merger with CSX despite a higher, hostile offer from Norfolk Southern.
Conrail has repeatedly rejected Norfolk Southern's bid, saying that CSX's offer provides more benefits.

"The Conrail board has determined that a sale to Norfolk Southern is not in the best interests of Conrail, and the Conrail board will not agree to a sale to Norfolk Southern," LeVan said in remarks prepared for delivery to the shareholders meeting.
LeVan said Conrail's board was not swayed by a proposal by Norfolk Southern to buy 9.9 percent of the company if shareholders defeated the measure, which was critical to the CSX union.

"I hope you all understand the Conrail board is fully committed to the CSX-Conrail merger and, regardless of speculation to the contrary, there can be no transaction with Norfolk Southern until 1999 at the earliest," he said.
The proposed merger pact between Conrail and CSX prohibits either party, should their pact fail, from merging with another company until 1999.
